mission.title: Bug Before Launch
mission.introduction: Your studio's game launches on Friday. Testers report that the game freezes when they open the map.

steps.prompt: It is Tuesday. What do you do first?

choices.text: Reproduce the freeze and read the logs.
choices.feedback: Good. You cannot fix what you cannot see. Most bug fixing starts here.

choices.text: Ask the testers exactly what they did before it froze.
choices.feedback: Testers often notice the pattern first. Clear questions save hours of guessing.

choices.text: Remove the map from the game for launch.
choices.feedback: It ships on time, but players lose a feature. Sometimes this is the right call, but try a fix first.

steps.prompt: You found it: the map loads every icon at once. A full fix takes two days.

choices.text: Load the icons in small batches over several frames.
choices.feedback: A classic performance fix. Players never notice the difference, and the freeze is gone.

choices.text: Tell the producer now and agree on a backup plan.
choices.feedback: Producers can plan around problems they know about. A surprise on Thursday hurts everyone.

choices.text: Redesign the map so it needs fewer icons.
choices.feedback: A design fix can beat a code fix. It also needs the artists on board, so talk to them early.

mission.title: Night Shift
mission.introduction: You are the nurse on a busy hospital ward. It is 2 a.m.

steps.prompt: Two patients call at once. One has pain after surgery. One wants a glass of water.

choices.text: Check the patient in pain first.
choices.feedback: Right. Nurses triage: the most urgent need comes first.

choices.text: Ask a colleague to bring the water while you check the pain.
choices.feedback: Good teamwork. Nobody waits long, and the urgent need is covered.

choices.text: Bring the water first because it is quick.
choices.feedback: Kind, but the patient in pain may be getting worse. Urgency comes first.

steps.prompt: The patient's pain is higher than normal and their heart rate is up.

choices.text: Record the readings and call the doctor.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Clear notes and fast escalation keep patients safe.

choices.text: Stay with the patient and keep them calm.
choices.feedback: Calm patients do better. Make sure the doctor is told as well.

choices.text: Check the medication chart for a missed dose.
choices.feedback: Careful thinking. A missed dose could explain the pain.

mission.title: Lights Out
mission.introduction: A small bakery calls you. Half of their lights and one oven have stopped working.

steps.prompt: You arrive at the bakery. What do you do first?

choices.text: Turn off power to that circuit and lock the panel.
choices.feedback: Safety first, always. Electricians lock out a circuit before they touch it.

choices.text: Ask the owner what happened just before it stopped.
choices.feedback: Customers often know the cause. "It stopped when we plugged in the new oven" is a big clue.

choices.text: Replace the breaker straight away.
choices.feedback: It might work, but you have not found the cause. The new breaker may trip again.

steps.prompt: The new oven needs more power than the old circuit can carry.

choices.text: Install a separate circuit for the oven.
choices.feedback: The right technical fix. Each heavy appliance gets the power it needs.

choices.text: Explain the options and costs to the owner.
choices.feedback: Owners trust electricians who explain clearly. They also decide faster.

choices.text: Plan the work for Monday, when the bakery is closed.
choices.feedback: Good planning. The bakery keeps selling, and you can work safely.

mission.title: The Sales Puzzle
mission.introduction: A bike shop's sales dropped by 20% last month. The owner wants to know why.

choices.text: Clean the data and check for missing days.
choices.feedback: Smart. Missing data can look exactly like a drop in sales.

choices.text: Compare this month with the same month last year.
choices.feedback: Seasons matter. Fewer people buy bikes in cold months.

choices.text: Interview the shop staff.
choices.feedback: Staff know things the data cannot show, like a closed road or a new shop nearby.

steps.prompt: You find that sales dropped for only one product: kids' bikes.

choices.text: Dig deeper into prices and stock for kids' bikes.
choices.feedback: The kids' bikes were out of stock for two weeks. Mystery solved.

choices.text: Make one clear chart and explain it in one sentence.
choices.feedback: Great analysis is useless if nobody understands it.

choices.text: Build a model to predict next month's sales.
choices.feedback: Useful later, but the owner needs an answer first.
